transcript.content: Hello, welcome. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, I’m here mostly because my regular doctor sent me. She’s been on me about my weight—saying it’s gotten too low, lower than she’s comfortable with—and now everyone seems to be making a big fuss over it. I mean, I know I’m lighter than I used to be, but to me it doesn’t feel like the emergency everybody’s acting like it is.

Honestly, part of me feels like being this light helps me keep going. I work in a shop, carpentry, and there’s a lot of moving around, bending, climbing, hauling things, being on my feet. I don’t like feeling slowed down or heavy or sluggish. So when people say, “You need to put weight back on,” I hear that, but I also think, well, I’m managing, aren’t I? I can still keep up with what I need to do. That’s sort of why I’m here—because my doctor insisted I come talk to someone about it.
Can you tell me more about how you’ve managed your eating and weight recently?

Lately it’s been… pretty structured, I guess, though I don’t always think of it that way. On days I’m in the workshop, especially, I don’t really stop for a proper meal. I’ll have tea, usually, and maybe a few bites of something if I feel like I need it or if it’s there, but I keep it very careful. Small. Enough that I can say I had something, but not so much that I feel thrown off.

It’s not that I’m trying to make a whole production of it. It’s just that when I’m working, stopping to sit down and eat a real meal feels unnecessary, and honestly it interrupts the rhythm of the day. Once I get going with the measurements and the cutting and sanding and moving between tasks, I don’t want to break that up. And eating more than that makes me feel like I’ve lost the control I had over the day somehow, like things get heavier or slower. So I tend to keep it to tea and just a little bit, and then I can keep moving and keep things in order.
Do you find yourself worried about gaining weight or becoming heavier than you are now, even if others might say you’re already at a healthy or low weight?

Yes… I do, though I don’t always like saying it that plainly. It’s not like I’m sitting there thinking about numbers every second, but if I eat something that feels heavy—like a proper rich meal, or the kinds of foods we used to make around the holidays, the buttery things, the casseroles, the pies, all of that—I can feel the worry start almost right away.

It’s this immediate thought of, well, now I’ve done it, now I’m going to gain, now I’m going to feel bigger and lose the grip I’ve worked so hard to keep. And I know people might say, “One meal doesn’t do that,” but in my head it doesn’t feel that simple. It feels like if I let myself have those foods, or if I get too comfortable eating that way, then I’ll slide into being heavier before I can stop it. So yes, I suppose I am worried about becoming heavier than I am now, even if other people think I shouldn’t be.
Have you ever done anything to try to get rid of calories or prevent weight gain after eating, such as making yourself sick, using laxatives, or exercising more than usual?

I’m not sure how to answer that exactly. I mean, I don’t… I don’t think of myself as doing something like that after eating, if you mean a specific thing where I eat and then immediately try to undo it.

I don’t make myself sick, no. And laxatives aren’t really part of anything for me. The exercise part is harder to answer, because my work is physical anyway—being in the shop, moving wood, carrying things, standing all day—so I’m active whether I mean to be or not. But I wouldn’t say I have some set thing where I eat and then go, right, now I have to burn this off. It’s more that I prefer to keep moving and not feel like food has made me heavy or slowed down. 

So… no, not in the way you’re describing, I don’t think.
Do you see yourself as heavier than you actually are, or do you feel like you need to lose more weight even when others say you're already too thin?

I don’t think I see myself as… I mean, I don’t look at myself and think I’m enormous, if that’s what you mean. But I do think I could stand to keep things where they are, or be a little more careful. And that’s where people seem to get upset with me.

My husband says it a lot now—too much, honestly. He’ll say I look too thin, that my face looks drawn, that my clothes hang differently. And the apprentices at the shop, they try to be polite about it, but I can tell. One of them made some comment about me needing a proper lunch, and another asked if I was feeling all right because I looked “small,” which just irritated me. I know they mean well, but it feels like everyone is watching and deciding they know better than I do.

I keep telling them I’m fine. I really do. I tell them people are confusing discipline with sickness. Because to me, being careful and keeping control of myself doesn’t automatically mean something is wrong. I’ve always believed you should be able to manage yourself, your habits, your body, the same way you manage good work—measure twice, don’t be sloppy, don’t overdo things. But when I do that with food or weight, suddenly everyone acts like I’ve lost all judgment.

So… yes, other people say I’m too thin. But I don’t quite see it that way. I feel like they’re making it into something bigger than it is.
Can you tell me about your current weight and whether you know what is considered a healthy weight for someone your height and age?

Well… I know it’s low. I mean, that’s the whole reason my doctor sent me here, really. She got very serious about it at the last appointment and said my weight had dropped to a point where she wasn’t comfortable just “keeping an eye on it” anymore. My husband has been fussing too, and then people at the shop started acting like I might snap in half if I carried a board wrong, which is humiliating, honestly.

As for what’s healthy for someone my height and age… I suppose I know there are charts and ranges and all of that. I’ve seen them. I know doctors have a number in mind where they want you to be. But I don’t know, it doesn’t feel as straightforward from inside my own body. Being lighter feels… easier, in some ways. I don’t feel weighed down. In the shop, I’m on my feet all day, moving around, bending, lifting, measuring, climbing around things, and when I’m lighter I feel like I can keep up better and not get slowed down.

So yes, I understand that everyone thinks it’s too low. I’m not pretending I haven’t heard that. I just don’t feel the same alarm about it that they seem to.
Has your focus on maintaining your weight or controlling your eating habits caused you any significant stress, or made it hard to do things you need or want to do in your daily life?

I wouldn’t say it stops me completely. I still go to the shop. I still open up, I still know what needs doing, I still check measurements and talk to customers and keep track of what everyone’s working on. So in that sense, no, it hasn’t made me unable to function.

But… it has changed the feel of things, if I’m being honest. My husband has started hovering more, and the apprentices have picked up on it too. If there’s heavier timber to move or something awkward to lift, one of them will sort of appear beside me before I’ve even asked, like they’re afraid I’m going to overdo it. Sometimes they just take it from me. And I know they probably think they’re helping, but it gets under my skin.

The shop has always been mine in a very particular way. Not just the business, but the rhythm of it—the carrying, the sorting, the physical part, knowing I can do the work myself and not be treated like something fragile. Lately it feels like everyone is watching me, checking whether I’ve eaten, checking whether I’m tired, checking whether I’m lifting too much. It makes the whole place feel less like my own space and more like I’m being managed in it.

So yes, I suppose it has caused stress. Not because I think I can’t do things, but because other people keep stepping in as if I can’t. And that’s been hard.
Do you find yourself thinking about food, weight, or eating even when other people aren’t bringing it up or when you’re not in the middle of working or eating?

I’m not sure how to answer that exactly. I mean… I don’t sit there all day thinking, “food, weight, food, weight,” like a drumbeat. It’s not as simple as that.

But I suppose I do notice it in the background sometimes. Like if I’m planning the day, I’ll think about what’s sensible, what won’t make me feel sluggish, what fits around work. But I don’t know if that’s unusual. Lots of people think about what they’re going to eat, don’t they? Especially when you’re busy and you don’t want to feel uncomfortable while you’re trying to work.

And weight… I don’t know. I’m aware of it. I’m aware that everyone else is aware of it, which makes it harder not to think about. Sometimes even when no one has said anything, I’m sort of bracing for someone to say something. But whether that means I’m preoccupied with it, I’m not sure. It feels more like trying to keep things orderly in my head, if that makes sense. Like checking that everything is where it should be.
Would you say that your overall sense of how you’re doing, or how you feel about yourself, depends a lot on how you feel about your weight or your body shape?

I’m not sure. That’s a hard one, because I don’t think of myself as someone who stands in front of the mirror all day judging every inch of myself, if that’s what you mean. I’m not… I don’t know, I’m not trying to look like someone in a magazine. At my age that would be a bit ridiculous anyway.

But I suppose how I feel in my body does affect how I feel in general. If I feel heavy or uncomfortable, or like my clothes are sitting wrong, it can put me in a foul mood. It makes me feel clumsy, like I’m taking up too much space or moving wrong. And when I feel lighter, I feel more in control, more capable somehow. Like I can move through the day without having to think about myself as much.

I don’t know if that means my whole sense of myself depends on it. I’d like to say no, because I’m more than that. I’ve built a business, I know my trade, I’ve raised a family, I’m not some silly girl who only cares about her figure. But… it does matter to me. Probably more than I’d like to admit. If I feel wrong in my body, it sort of colors everything else, even if I’m trying to get on with things.
Have you noticed any changes in your menstrual cycle, such as periods becoming irregular or stopping altogether?

Well… no, not really in the way you mean, I don’t think. At my age that’s not something I’m tracking month to month anymore, so it’s a bit hard to answer like it’s a current symptom or a recent change.

I mean, I can’t say I’ve noticed periods becoming irregular or stopping because that isn’t really part of my life now. If you’re asking whether there’s been some obvious change lately that I’ve connected to all of this, then no, I wouldn’t say I’ve noticed anything like that. It’s not something I’ve had reason to keep an eye on, honestly.
Would you say that your overall sense of self-worth or how you judge yourself is strongly tied to how you see your body weight or shape?

I suppose I still don’t know how to separate those things neatly. “Self-worth” sounds very big, doesn’t it? Like whether I think I’m a decent person, or whether I’ve done anything worthwhile with my life. And I’d like to say that comes from other things — my work, being reliable, doing a job properly, not letting people down.

But if I’m honest, the way I feel about my body does get tangled up in how I judge myself. If I feel like I’ve got it under control, I feel steadier, more competent. If I feel like my body is wrong somehow, or bigger than it should be, then I start feeling… I don’t know, disappointed in myself. Irritated. Like I’ve failed at something basic that other people don’t even have to think about.

I don’t think it’s just vanity. That’s the part I get defensive about, because it sounds so shallow when you say it out loud. It’s more like my body becomes evidence of whether I’m disciplined or whether I’m slipping. And once I feel I’m slipping there, it makes me doubt myself more generally. So yes, maybe it is tied together more strongly than I’d prefer to admit.
Do you intentionally restrict the amount of food you eat, such as skipping meals or setting strict limits on calories, in order to control your weight?

Yes… I suppose I do, though I don’t always think of it as “restricting” in the moment. On workshop days especially, I get into this pattern where I’ll just have tea, and maybe a few careful bites of something if I feel I ought to, but I won’t stop for what you’d call a proper meal.

Part of it is that once I’m working, stopping feels disruptive. I’ve got the rhythm of the day, the measurements in my head, tools out, dust everywhere, and sitting down to eat feels unnecessary, almost like it would throw everything off. But if I’m being honest, it’s also because eating more than that makes me feel like I’ve lost the control I had over the day. So I keep it very limited. Tea feels safe and manageable, and a small amount of food feels like enough to keep going without upsetting things.

I know that probably sounds quite rigid when I say it out loud. At the time I tell myself I’m just busy, or that lunch is a nuisance, but there is definitely an element of keeping it contained so my weight doesn’t creep up.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences undue influence of body weight or shape on self-evaluation, which is a key feature distinguishing Anorexia Nervosa (F50.0) from Atypical Anorexia Nervosa (F50.01) and Unspecified Feeding or Eating Disorder (F50.89).
doctor.question: Would you say that your overall sense of how you’re doing, or how you feel about yourself, depends a lot on how you feel about your weight or your body shape?

target_item.reason: The question is about whether self-worth or overall self-evaluation depends on weight or body shape, which is not directly covered by the provided symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure. That’s a hard one, because I don’t think of myself as someone who stands in front of the mirror all day judging every inch of myself, if that’s what you mean. I’m not… I don’t know, I’m not trying to look like someone in a magazine. At my age that would be a bit ridiculous anyway.

But I suppose how I feel in my body does affect how I feel in general. If I feel heavy or uncomfortable, or like my clothes are sitting wrong, it can put me in a foul mood. It makes me feel clumsy, like I’m taking up too much space or moving wrong. And when I feel lighter, I feel more in control, more capable somehow. Like I can move through the day without having to think about myself as much.

I don’t know if that means my whole sense of myself depends on it. I’d like to say no, because I’m more than that. I’ve built a business, I know my trade, I’ve raised a family, I’m not some silly girl who only cares about her figure. But… it does matter to me. Probably more than I’d like to admit. If I feel wrong in my body, it sort of colors everything else, even if I’m trying to get on with things.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences amenorrhea (absence of menstrual periods), which would help differentiate between anorexia nervosa (F50.0), atypical anorexia nervosa (F50.01), and other eating disorders such as F50.1 or F50.2.
doctor.question: Have you noticed any changes in your menstrual cycle, such as periods becoming irregular or stopping altogether?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about menstrual cycle changes or amenorrhea, which is not covered by any item in the provided symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well… no, not really in the way you mean, I don’t think. At my age that’s not something I’m tracking month to month anymore, so it’s a bit hard to answer like it’s a current symptom or a recent change.

I mean, I can’t say I’ve noticed periods becoming irregular or stopping because that isn’t really part of my life now. If you’re asking whether there’s been some obvious change lately that I’ve connected to all of this, then no, I wouldn’t say I’ve noticed anything like that. It’s not something I’ve had reason to keep an eye on, honestly.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences undue influence of body weight or shape on self-evaluation, which is a key feature distinguishing Anorexia Nervosa (F50.0) from other feeding or eating disorders.
doctor.question: Would you say that your overall sense of self-worth or how you judge yourself is strongly tied to how you see your body weight or shape?

target_item.reason: The question is about whether self-worth or self-judgment is overly tied to body weight or shape, which is not directly covered by the listed symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
I suppose I still don’t know how to separate those things neatly. “Self-worth” sounds very big, doesn’t it? Like whether I think I’m a decent person, or whether I’ve done anything worthwhile with my life. And I’d like to say that comes from other things — my work, being reliable, doing a job properly, not letting people down.

But if I’m honest, the way I feel about my body does get tangled up in how I judge myself. If I feel like I’ve got it under control, I feel steadier, more competent. If I feel like my body is wrong somehow, or bigger than it should be, then I start feeling… I don’t know, disappointed in myself. Irritated. Like I’ve failed at something basic that other people don’t even have to think about.

I don’t think it’s just vanity. That’s the part I get defensive about, because it sounds so shallow when you say it out loud. It’s more like my body becomes evidence of whether I’m disciplined or whether I’m slipping. And once I feel I’m slipping there, it makes me doubt myself more generally. So yes, maybe it is tied together more strongly than I’d prefer to admit.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient engages in restrictive eating behaviors specifically aimed at weight loss or control, beyond just 'small' portions or 'structured' eating.
doctor.question: Do you intentionally restrict the amount of food you eat, such as skipping meals or setting strict limits on calories, in order to control your weight?

target_item.name: Restrictive_Intake
target_item.manifestation: On workshop days I usually just have tea and maybe a few careful bites of something, because stopping for a real meal feels unnecessary and throws off the control I’ve got over the day.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about intentionally limiting food intake, skipping meals, or setting strict calorie limits to control weight, which directly matches restrictive intake.

patient.answer:
Yes… I suppose I do, though I don’t always think of it as “restricting” in the moment. On workshop days especially, I get into this pattern where I’ll just have tea, and maybe a few careful bites of something if I feel I ought to, but I won’t stop for what you’d call a proper meal.

Part of it is that once I’m working, stopping feels disruptive. I’ve got the rhythm of the day, the measurements in my head, tools out, dust everywhere, and sitting down to eat feels unnecessary, almost like it would throw everything off. But if I’m being honest, it’s also because eating more than that makes me feel like I’ve lost the control I had over the day. So I keep it very limited. Tea feels safe and manageable, and a small amount of food feels like enough to keep going without upsetting things.

I know that probably sounds quite rigid when I say it out loud. At the time I tell myself I’m just busy, or that lunch is a nuisance, but there is definitely an element of keeping it contained so my weight doesn’t creep up.

inference.note: This turn confirmed intentional food restriction to control weight, which is a key criterion for anorexia nervosa (F50.0). No behaviors supporting purging or other types seen in F50.1 or F50.2 were endorsed.
